name: AI Glossary
note: Term list taken from the Stanford HAI AI Glossary. Definitions are paraphrased in original wording (not copied). Refer to the source page for the official text.

terms.definition: An attack where someone secretly tampers with how a model is trained or copied so the resulting model behaves in a harmful or compromised way.
A hypothetical AI that can learn and reason across almost any task at human level or better, instead of being good at one narrow thing.
AI that works like an agent: it takes a goal, plans steps, uses tools (browser, code, APIs), reacts to feedback and keeps going until the task is done.
Making sure an AI's goals and behavior match what humans actually intend and value.
Standard tests used to score and compare AI systems on tasks like Q&A, coding, vision or following instructions.
The ability to work with AI well and responsibly: knowing what it can and can't do, using it effectively, checking its outputs and staying ethical.
The field focused on making AI reliable and harmless, even when it is powerful, widely used or facing unexpected situations.
The combined layers of software, hardware and compute that support everything from building to running AI.
The full pipeline for an AI system: prepare data, train, test, deploy and maintain, with each stage feeding the next.
A step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem, like a recipe.
When many organizations rely on the same or very similar AI models, algorithms or data, so they share the same blind spots and failures.
A group of AI systems or agents that share information and coordinate actions as if acting as one collective.
Machines built to do things that normally need human intelligence. The term was coined in 1955 by Stanford's John McCarthy.
A technique that lets a neural network focus on the most relevant parts of its input when producing an output.
Technology carrying out tasks exactly as humans have explicitly instructed it, with no goal-setting of its own.
The way neural networks learn from errors: the error is traced backward through the layers to see which weights caused it, then those are adjusted.
Graph-based models that use probabilities to show how variables influence each other.
When an AI system produces results that unfairly favor or disadvantage certain groups of people.
Datasets so large that normal tools can't handle them, often analyzed with AI to find patterns.
A program that simulates conversation with people through text or voice.
Software (also called proprietary) whose code is kept private and can't be freely viewed, modified or reused.
The AI field that lets computers interpret and understand images and video.
The maximum amount of input (like text) a model can take in and consider at one time.
Training by comparing similar and different examples so the model learns what makes things alike or distinct.
Growing a training set by making altered copies of existing data instead of collecting new data.
Using statistics and machine learning to uncover patterns in large datasets.
An attack where bad actors insert, change or mislabel training data to corrupt what a model learns.
An algorithm that predicts by asking a chain of yes/no questions about the data until it reaches an answer.
A kind of machine learning that uses large, many-layered neural networks to learn complex patterns automatically.
Generative models that create content like images by learning to remove noise step by step.
Simplifying data by cutting the number of variables while keeping the most important information.
Lists of numbers (vectors) that represent words, images or other items so their meaning or traits can be compared mathematically.
Combining several models to get a prediction that is more accurate and stable than any single one.
Building and using AI in line with human values, fairness, transparency and societal well-being.
Older AI programs that mimic human experts using a knowledge base and if-then rules.
Methods that make an AI's decisions understandable to people instead of leaving it a black box.
Training a shared model across many devices or servers while the data stays where it is.
Teaching a model a new task with just a handful of examples.
Taking an already trained model and training it further on task- or domain-specific data.
Very large models trained on broad data that can be adapted to many different tasks and applications.
A general-purpose AI model at or near the cutting edge of current capability.
AI that creates new content such as text, images, music, code or video.
Two neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, that compete so the generator learns to produce realistic fake data.
A family of large language models built on the transformer architecture that generate human-like text from prompts.
A chip originally made for graphics that does many calculations in parallel, which makes it ideal for training AI.
When an AI confidently produces information that is wrong, misleading or made up.
An approach that puts human needs, values and well-being first when developing and deploying AI.
The study and practice of how people use and engage with computer systems.
AI systems where a person provides feedback or can step in as part of the process.
A setting chosen by the builder before training starts, rather than learned by the model.
A giant tech company with huge data-center networks that can quickly scale compute, storage and cloud services.
When a trained model is used to make predictions or decisions on new, unseen data.
How well humans can understand why an AI reached a particular decision or prediction.
A simple algorithm that classifies or predicts by looking at the closest similar examples.
A structured database that stores facts as connected entities and the relationships between them.
An AI trained on massive amounts of text so it can understand and generate human-like language.
A compressed, abstract space where data is encoded so that its essential features and patterns are captured.
Practices for managing the whole lifecycle of LLM-based apps in production.
A formula that measures how far a model's predictions are from the correct answers.
A branch of AI where computers learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
A model where the next event depends only on the current state, not on how you got there.
Combining ML, software engineering and DevOps to deploy, monitor and maintain models reliably in production.
A simplified mathematical or computational representation of a real-world system, used to predict or understand patterns.
When a model's performance gets worse over time because real-world data changes from what it was trained on.
AI that can handle several data types at once, such as text, images, audio and video.
The AI field focused on letting computers understand, interpret and generate human language.
A model loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of connected artificial neurons that pass information along.
A method that tweaks a model's settings step by step so it makes fewer mistakes.
When a model memorizes its training data, including noise, and then performs poorly on new data.
A model whose weights, code, training data (or an auditable account of it) and tools are all available to download, inspect, modify and reproduce.
A model whose trained weights are publicly released for anyone to download, though other parts may stay private.
Software whose design and code are freely available for anyone to see and use.
An internal value in a model that is learned and adjusted during training.
Using data, statistics and ML to forecast future outcomes or trends.
Carefully writing instructions (prompts) to steer a language model toward the output you want.
A security attack where malicious input tricks an LLM into doing something unintended.
A technique where a language model first looks up relevant external, up-to-date information and then uses it to write a better answer.
An AI built to solve hard problems by working through a logical, step-by-step chain of thought.
Learning by trial and error, where an agent acts in an environment and improves based on rewards.
The principles, frameworks and practices guiding ethical and safe development and use of AI.
The field combining engineering and computer science (increasingly AI) to build machines that perform physical tasks.
The ability to understand and reason about the 3D physical world, including how objects relate, move and interact.
A training method where the model creates its own puzzles from raw data and learns by solving them.
Figuring out the meaning of language by looking at relationships among words, phrases and symbols.
Predictable relationships showing how model performance improves as model size, data and compute grow.
Training on labeled examples, where each input comes paired with the correct answer.
Artificially generated data made by algorithms or simulations instead of real-world collection.
A container for numbers arranged in multiple dimensions, like a spreadsheet extended to many axes.
Splitting text into small units (tokens: words, word pieces or characters) that a language model can process.
Earlier AI built on hand-coded rules, logic and human-defined knowledge rather than learning from data.
The examples (text, images, audio, etc.) used to teach a machine learning model a task.
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a related task.
A neural network architecture that uses attention to relate all parts of the input at once instead of one after another.
Alan Turing's 1950 idea for judging whether a machine's behavior is indistinguishable from a human's.
Training on unlabeled data so the model finds patterns and structure by itself.
A database built to store and quickly search vector representations of text, images or audio.
A transformer adapted from language tasks to process and analyze images.
The numbers in a neural network that set how strongly neurons connect and so shape how the model processes information.
A model handling tasks or categories it was never explicitly trained on, using its general knowledge.
